--- title: "Regression performance measures" description: "RMSE, MAE, R² and MAPE disagree about which model is best, and each disagreement tells you something specific about your counts." order: 3 categories: [validation, metrics, regression] --- ## Why this matters A performance measure is a statement about which mistakes you mind. RMSE says a single station predicted ten out is worse than a hundred stations predicted one out. MAE says they are the same. Neither is correct in the abstract; they are answers to different questions, and on marine count data they routinely disagree about which model wins. That disagreement is not a nuisance to be resolved by picking a default. It is diagnostic information, and this page reads it. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ## The idea For a continuous or count response, with $y_i$ observed and $\hat y_i$ predicted at station $i$: | Measure | What it is | What it minds | | --- | --- | --- | | **RMSE** | root of the mean squared error | large misses, quadratically | | **MAE** | mean absolute error | every unit of error equally | | **R²** (`rsq`) | squared correlation of $y$ and $\hat y$ | *pattern* only — blind to bias | | **R²** (`rsq_trad`) | $1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}$ | pattern and bias, relative to the response's own spread | | **MAPE** | mean absolute *percentage* error | errors relative to the observed value | The two R²s are not a typo. `yardstick::rsq()` is the squared correlation and `rsq_trad()` is the proportion of variance explained. For an ordinary least-squares fit on its own training data they are identical, which is why most people have never had to notice. On held-out predictions from anything else they are not, and the gap between them is worth reading. ## Worked example Five models of the same counts, each scored on pooled out-of-fold predictions from the same ten folds so the comparison is exact. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() d <- survey |> dplyr::select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu, substrate, season, longitude, latitude) |> drop_na() formula_env <- abundance ~ poly(depth_m, 2) + poly(temperature_c, 2) + log1p(chlorophyll_mg_m3) + salinity_psu + substrate + season + longitude + latitude fitters <- list( `mean only` = \(tr, te) rep(mean(tr$abundance), nrow(te)), `Poisson GLM` = \(tr, te) predict(glm(formula_env, tr, family = poisson), te, type = "response"), `negative binomial` = \(tr, te) predict(glm.nb(formula_env, tr), te, type = "response"), `log-transformed lm` = \(tr, te) expm1(predict(lm(update(formula_env, log1p(abundance) ~ .), tr), te)), `random forest` = \(tr, te) predict(ranger(abundance ~ ., tr, num.trees = 500, seed = 1), te)$predictions ) set.seed(61) folds <- vfold_cv(d, v = 10) out_of_fold <- imap_dfr(fitters, \(f, name) { imap_dfr(folds$splits, \(s, i) { tr <- analysis(s); te <- assessment(s) tibble(model = name, fold = i, obs = te$abundance, pred = f(tr, te)) }) }) nrow(out_of_fold) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 3600 ``` ::: ::: The `log-transformed lm` is the common shortcut for skewed counts: fit an ordinary linear model to `log1p(abundance)`, then undo the transformation with `expm1()`. Keep an eye on it. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scores <- out_of_fold |> summarise(RMSE = rmse_vec(obs, pred), MAE = mae_vec(obs, pred), rsq = rsq_vec(obs, pred), rsq_trad = rsq_trad_vec(obs, pred), `total predicted / total observed` = sum(pred) / sum(obs), .by = model) scores |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | RMSE| MAE| rsq| rsq_trad| total predicted / total observed| |:------------------|-----:|-----:|-----:|--------:|--------------------------------:| |mean only | 4.826| 3.411| 0.012| -0.003| 1.000| |Poisson GLM | 4.216| 2.899| 0.237| 0.234| 1.002| |negative binomial | 4.215| 2.891| 0.236| 0.235| 0.998| |log-transformed lm | 4.461| 2.783| 0.224| 0.143| 0.694| |random forest | 4.363| 3.016| 0.184| 0.180| 1.034|
::: ::: ## What the results mean **RMSE and MAE pick different winners.** The negative binomial has the lowest RMSE at 4.215. The log-transformed linear model has the lowest MAE at 2.783 — and it is *fourth* of five on RMSE. That is not noise; it is the two measures doing their jobs. The log model was fitted to minimise error on the log scale, where the crowded low counts dominate. Back on the count scale it predicts low almost everywhere, which is cheap under MAE (most stations really do hold a handful of individuals) and expensive under RMSE (the few stations holding thirty are missed badly). The last column shows the damage: **it predicts 69% of the total abundance actually observed.** For a survey whose purpose is a stock estimate, that is a disqualifying flaw that MAE rewarded. ::: {.callout-warning} ## `rsq()` cannot see that The log model's `rsq` is 0.224, close to the best in the table. Its `rsq_trad` is 0.143. The gap is the bias: squared correlation is unchanged if you multiply every prediction by 0.69, because correlation does not care about scale or offset. If you report `rsq()` — which is what `metric_set(rsq)` and `collect_metrics()` give you by default — you can publish a model that under-counts the stock by a third and still show a respectable R². Report `rsq_trad()` as well, or report the ratio of totals directly. ::: ### RMSE is mostly a measurement of a few stations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} worst_share <- function(data, error, fractions = c(0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25)) { e <- sort(error(data$obs, data$pred), decreasing = TRUE) tibble(`worst stations` = scales::percent(fractions, accuracy = 1), share = map_dbl(fractions, \(p) sum(e[seq_len(round(p * length(e)))]) / sum(e))) } nb <- filter(out_of_fold, model == "negative binomial") left_join( worst_share(nb, \(o, p) (o - p)^2) |> rename(`share of squared error` = share), worst_share(nb, \(o, p) abs(o - p)) |> rename(`share of absolute error` = share), by = "worst stations" ) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) scales::percent(x, accuracy = 0.1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|worst stations |share of squared error |share of absolute error | |:--------------|:----------------------|:-----------------------| |1% |23.5% |6.8% | |2% |32.9% |11.2% | |5% |50.7% |21.8% | |10% |65.2% |34.2% | |25% |85.4% |59.4% |
::: ::: Seven stations out of 720 — the worst 1% — account for about a quarter of the squared error the RMSE is built from. The worst 5% account for half of it. Under absolute error the same 5% account for a fifth. So when you compare two models by RMSE on aggregating species, you are largely comparing how they handle a handful of big hauls. That may be exactly right — a model for fishery management had better get the dense patches right — but it should be a decision, not an accident. ### What MAPE would have you do MAPE divides each error by the observed value, which has two consequences on count data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c(stations = nrow(nb), `stations with zero caught` = sum(nb$obs == 0), `MAPE on the rest (%)` = mape_vec(nb$obs[nb$obs > 0], nb$pred[nb$obs > 0])) |> round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> stations stations with zero caught MAPE on the rest (%) #> 720.0 157.0 91.6 ``` ::: ::: The first consequence is that it does not exist. Dividing by an observed count of zero is undefined, and 157 of these 720 stations caught nothing — so MAPE can only be computed after silently discarding the fifth of the survey that is most informative about where the species is not. The second is worse. Under-prediction can cost at most 100% per station; over-prediction is unbounded. We can see which way that pushes by taking one model's predictions and multiplying them all by a constant. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} non_zero <- filter(nb, obs > 0) scales_tried <- seq(0.3, 1.6, by = 0.01) curves <- tibble( scale = scales_tried, RMSE = map_dbl(scales_tried, \(k) rmse_vec(nb$obs, nb$pred * k)), MAE = map_dbl(scales_tried, \(k) mae_vec(nb$obs, nb$pred * k)), MAPE = map_dbl(scales_tried, \(k) mape_vec(non_zero$obs, non_zero$pred * k)) ) |> pivot_longer(-scale, names_to = "measure", values_to = "value") |> mutate(measure = factor(measure, c("RMSE", "MAE", "MAPE")), relative = value / min(value), .by = measure) minima <- slice_min(curves, relative, by = measure) ggplot(curves, aes(scale, relative)) + geom_line(aes(colour = measure), linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(data = minima, aes(colour = measure), size = 3) + geom_text(data = minima, aes(label = sprintf("best at %.2f", scale)), vjust = -1.1, size = 3.4) + facet_wrap(~measure, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0.4, 1.6, 0.2)) + scale_colour_ml() + labs(x = "multiply every prediction by", y = "measure, relative to its own best", title = "Three measures, three different ideal predictions") + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![What happens to three measures when every prediction from the negative binomial model is multiplied by a constant. Each panel is scaled to its own best value. RMSE bottoms out at 0.98, essentially where the model already is. MAE bottoms out at 0.74. MAPE, computed on the 563 non-zero stations, bottoms out at 0.47 — it would have you halve every prediction you believe in.](regression-metrics_files/figure-html/fig-scaling-1.png){#fig-scaling fig-alt='Three curves on a shared horizontal axis labelled multiply every prediction by, running from 0.3 to 1.6, each in its own panel stacked vertically and each scaled so its lowest value is 1. The top panel, RMSE, is a symmetric U with a dot at its base at 0.98. The middle panel, MAE, is a shallower U with its dot at 0.74. The bottom panel, MAPE, is almost flat from 0.3 to 0.6 with its dot at 0.47, then climbs steeply and without turning to 2.6 times its best value by the right-hand edge — an asymmetric curve, punishing over-prediction far more than under-prediction.' width=1400} ::: ::: MAPE prefers a model that predicts 47% of what the negative binomial believes. MAE prefers 74%. RMSE is minimised at 0.98 — essentially where the model already is. Notice the shape as well as the minimum: MAPE is nearly flat to the left of its best point and climbs steeply to the right, which is the asymmetry made visible. A measure that systematically rewards under-prediction has no place in abundance work, and this is why. ::: {.callout-important} ## The fold-to-fold spread, and why you may not compare across schemes Section 6 ran into this three times. Here it is directly: the *same* negative binomial model, scored fold by fold on the same ten folds. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} by_fold <- nb |> summarise(`sd of counts in fold` = sd(obs), RMSE = rmse_vec(obs, pred), rsq_trad = rsq_trad_vec(obs, pred), .by = fold) by_fold |> summarise(lowest_rmse = min(RMSE), highest_rmse = max(RMSE), lowest_rsq_trad = min(rsq_trad), highest_rsq_trad = max(rsq_trad), `correlation of fold sd with fold RMSE` = cor(`sd of counts in fold`, RMSE)) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| lowest_rmse| highest_rmse| lowest_rsq_trad| highest_rsq_trad| correlation of fold sd with fold RMSE| |-----------:|------------:|---------------:|----------------:|-------------------------------------:| | 3.509| 5.923| -0.425| 0.462| 0.777|
::: ::: One model, one dataset: RMSE between 3.51 and 5.92, and `rsq_trad` between **−0.42 and +0.46** — from worse than predicting the fold's own mean to explaining nearly half its variance. The last number explains it. Fold RMSE correlates 0.78 with how spread out that fold's counts happen to be. So an RMSE is a property of the model *and* of the rows it was scored on. Compare RMSEs only when both models saw exactly the same rows — which is why every comparison in this section pools the out-of-fold predictions first. ::: ## Where this breaks down Every measure here treats a prediction as a single number. Count models produce a whole predicted distribution, and collapsing it to its mean throws away the part a survey often cares about most — the chance of finding nothing at all. The *proper scoring rules* that grade a whole predicted distribution (log score, CRPS, Poisson deviance) are the right tool there, and `yardstick::poisson_log_loss()` is the easiest entry point. None of these measures is on the scale of a decision either. "RMSE 4.2" does not say whether the survey design is adequate. Turning a measure into a decision is [the last page of this section](choosing-a-metric.qmd). ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - RMSE and MAE disagreed about the best of five models here, and the disagreement was informative: the MAE winner under-predicted total abundance by 31%. - `rsq()` is a squared correlation and cannot see bias. Report `rsq_trad()`, or the ratio of predicted to observed totals, alongside it. - On these counts the worst 1% of stations carry a quarter of the squared error and the worst 5% carry half. RMSE is mostly about the big hauls. - MAPE is undefined wherever the count is zero, and on the rest it is minimised by predicting 47% of what you believe. Do not use it for abundance. - The same model scored 3.51 to 5.92 RMSE across ten folds. Compare metrics only on identical rows. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Refit the log-transformed model with the standard smearing correction (multiply the back-transformed prediction by the mean of `exp(residual)`). How much of the 31% shortfall does it recover, and what does it cost on MAE? 2. Add `poisson_log_loss()` to the scores table. Does it rank the five models like RMSE, like MAE, or like neither?
